# Talk about making love before you do it

From here on, when I say making love, I'm talking about two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected, using their bodies as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced this, it may be like trying to explain the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know. That’s another conversation, and I'd suggest reading my inner child reparenting guide.

Having sex is just the physical act, whether that connection is there or not. But sometimes it can create the connection also.

That last part matters because the act may change the connection. But most couples wait until they’re already having sex before they talk honestly about it. By then a truthful answer might interrupt something that has begun. Earlier, the conversation can still go places the later one often can’t. Having it is already part of the difference between making love together and merely having sex.

Some things you may know now. What does sex mean to you—recreation, bonding, sacred practice, stress relief, all of those, or something else? What do you actually desire? What helps your body feel safe? Are there kinks or particular dynamics that matter? What has your history taught you about your erotic wiring? What reliably doesn't work? How often do you each imagine wanting sex?

Some answers you may not know yet. A lot of people can’t answer cleanly because they don’t know. That’s still an answer. *I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out honestly with you* is a much better beginning than silently assuming the bodies will somehow negotiate everything on their own.

The way two people handle that uncertainty tells me something already. Sexual compatibility isn’t just whether two bodies fit. It’s whether two people can stay honest while maximally exposed. If you can talk frankly before your clothes come off, you’ve practiced some of the trust, attention, and willingness to be seen that making love requires.

The frequency question can come back differently with time. In a long relationship, one person usually wants more sex, less sex, or different sex for at least some stretch. What would that mismatch mean, and how might you handle it? It’s one of the great factories of quiet resentment. Talking before either person is hurt won’t solve it in advance, but it gives you somewhere to begin.

# Tough Love

Romantic love ain't easy, but it is priceless, and the things that actually make it work are not very marketable. I can't sell you the fix with one click or one monthly subscription to my love class. (Just kidding, click here!) It's worth every penny if you ask me, but I can’t give you a formula that makes it stay, aside from the obvious 1+1=2.

Making it work takes both people. That's rare, and probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history.

One of the best books that makes that point today might be the one I was reading with K: The Spirit of Intimacy, by Sobonfu Somé. Somé is coming from the Dagara tribe in Burkina Faso. To her people, marriage is an arranged, ritualized spiritual and communal responsibility. They're suspicious of romance.

One of Somé's ideas fits what I'm trying to say. Two people come together, and something larger than either person appears between them. She calls it the spirit of the relationship. I don’t think either lover owns it. Nobody can command it to stay.

At our best, we serve it. We tell the truth, keep doing our own inner play & work (pl/ork), ask the community for help, and listen for what the relationship is becoming. When we start thinking we own it or deserve it, that presumptuousness tends to push it away.

My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit. They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly. I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn't have articulated that since I didn't even have that concept at the time. Also reminiscent of Somé, they also wore rose-colored glasses and taught me that everybody was basically good. So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.

It took me many decades to figure out what probably everyone else already knows: real private pathology exists. But it festers like mold when the environment is perfect for it.

The dominant culture helps make that environment. It seals two people together, calls that privacy, and tells one person to become lover, family, community, therapist, and future. When damage appears, the culture calls it a purely private failure.

The romantic myths become real because we co-create them. We treat jealousy as proof of love. We act as if feelings can be promised forever, conflict should stay hidden, and a relationship failed if it ended.

None of those are natural laws, but we suffer inside them anyway and walk blindly into our first, second, third, fourth, and fifth marriages!

Speaking of which, I wish I’d prioritized understanding the basic fears, desires, traumas, values, strengths, and weaknesses of the women I got close to in a more conscious manner. Instead, I often went with the flow of conversation and hanging out until closeness had built itself before we had decided what it meant.

On the other hand, with H., maybe we had the opposite problem. We reached real depth quickly. That depth kept pulling us toward romantic partnership even though, instinctually, we felt more like family. Depth is powerful, but you still have to ask what kind of relationship you’re actually building.

Maybe this whole article is the rest of the sentence my dad gave me when I was five. And maybe I wrote it for my son, Bear, who sadly, I last saw when he was about five.

Bear, sex can be what you do when you’re older and find a friend you want to have children with.

Learn who she is before closeness makes the decision for you, and let her learn who you are. Keep friends around who know both of you. Don’t ask one woman to become your whole village.

Don't assume she loves you just because she wants you. Possession and commitment are not the same thing. If the relationship is real, treat it as something sacred without pretending you own the outcome.

That’s what I wish my dad had added. That’s what I’m trying to give you here.
